Here is a full classification of all 13 assertions across the two axes you asked about — **information quality** (primary vs. secondary vs. indeterminate) and **document type** (original vs. derivative).

---

## Document Type: Original vs. Derivative

This is a property of the **source**, not the individual assertion. All assertions from a given source share its classification.

| Source | Document | Type | Assertions |
|---|---|---|---|
| **src_001** | 1850 Census — FamilySearch image | **Original** | a_001–a_005 |
| **src_002** | 1850 Census — Ancestry index | **Derivative** | a_006–a_007 |
| **src_003** | 1860 Census — FamilySearch image | **Original** | a_008–a_010 |
| **src_004** | 1908 Death Certificate | **Original** | a_011–a_013 |

The Ancestry index (src_002) is the only derivative here — it is a transcription of the same underlying NARA original, not an independent record. The FamilySearch census images are digital reproductions of NARA microfilm, which are treated as original because we are working from the image of the original record. The death certificate is an original government document created at the time of the event.

---

## Information Quality: Primary, Secondary, or Indeterminate

This is a property of each **assertion**, based on whether the informant had firsthand knowledge of the specific fact.

### Primary information
*(Informant had firsthand knowledge — a witness to the event)*

| Assertion | Fact | Source | Why Primary |
|---|---|---|---|
| **a_003** | Residence, Schuylkill Co., 1850 | 1850 Census (orig.) | The enumerator physically visited the dwelling — a direct witness to residence |
| **a_011** | Death, 12 March 1908 | 1908 Death Cert. (orig.) | Attending physician signed the certificate — present at or near the time of death |

### Secondary information
*(Informant reported facts they did not personally witness)*

| Assertion | Fact | Source | Why Secondary |
|---|---|---|---|
| **a_012** | Birth, 1845, Pennsylvania | 1908 Death Cert. (orig.) | Informant is James Brown (son-in-law) — reporting Patrick's birth 63+ years after the event with no firsthand knowledge |
| **a_013** | Father: Thomas Flynn | 1908 Death Cert. (orig.) | Same informant — reporting his father-in-law's parentage, information he could only have been told, not witnessed |

### Indeterminate information
*(Cannot determine whether the informant had firsthand knowledge)*

| Assertion | Fact | Source | Why Indeterminate |
|---|---|---|---|
| **a_001** | Name "Patrick Flynn" | 1850 Census (orig.) | Informant unknown — likely a household member but possibly a neighbor; enumerator did not identify who answered |
| **a_002** | Birth, ~1845, Ireland | 1850 Census (orig.) | Same unknown informant; could be Thomas Flynn (would know his son's birthplace) or a neighbor who would not |
| **a_004** | Relationship in Thomas Flynn household | 1850 Census (orig.) | 1850 census did not record relationships — this is researcher inference, no identified informant at all |
| **a_005** | Name "Thomas Flynn" | 1850 Census (orig.) | Informant unknown; Thomas likely reported his own name but this cannot be confirmed |
| **a_006** | Name "Patrick Flynn" | 1850 Census (deriv.) | Ancestry transcriber copied from original — informant chain is once-removed from the original unknown informant |
| **a_007** | Birth, ~1845, Ireland | 1850 Census (deriv.) | Same as a_006 |
| **a_008** | Name "Patrick Flynn" | 1860 Census (orig.) | Informant unknown — same reasoning as a_001 |
| **a_009** | Birth, ~1845, Ireland | 1860 Census (orig.) | Informant unknown — same reasoning as a_002 |
| **a_010** | Relationship in Thomas Flynn household | 1860 Census (orig.) | Researcher inference — 1860 census also did not record relationships (that column wasn't added until 1880) |

---

## Key Takeaways for Your Research

1. **Sparse primary information.** Only two assertions carry primary information quality — one census residence fact and the death event itself. Most of what we know about Patrick comes from indeterminate census facts.

2. **The death certificate is a split document.** As an original source, it is excellent for the death facts (primary). But for birth and parentage facts, the informant (son-in-law James Brown) is secondary — he had no firsthand knowledge of events 63 years prior. This is the most important thing to keep in mind when weighing a_013 ("Father: Thomas Flynn").

3. **The Ancestry assertions (a_006, a_007) add almost nothing.** They duplicate facts already drawn from the FamilySearch original, with an additional layer of transcription risk. Their value is solely in confirming the original was not misread.

4. **The open conflict (c_001) — Ireland vs. Pennsylvania birthplace** — is a direct consequence of the information quality gap: indeterminate census informants (likely household members, closer to the facts) vs. a secondary death certificate informant (son-in-law). The censuses win on both proximity and contemporaneity.
